books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, January 1, 1831

stimulus.source_note: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. . . . I am in earnest — I will not equivocate — I will not excuse — I will not retreat a single inch — AND I WILL BE HEARD.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Garrison’s promise to “not retreat a single inch” best illustrates which approach to ending slavery?

options.text: Gradual emancipation, with enslaved people freed over many years.
options.misconception: Background from the books: gradual emancipation was the older, slower path favored by some earlier reformers; Garrison rejects anything gradual here.

options.text: Immediate abolition, demanded at once and without compromise.
Colonization, sending freed Black Americans to Africa.
options.misconception: Background from the books: colonization was the American Colonization Society’s plan; Garrison attacked it, and his words here demand an end to slavery itself.

options.text: Leaving slavery alone and letting it die out on its own.
options.misconception: Garrison demands action now, not patience; waiting for slavery to fade is the opposite of his pledge.

rationales.A: Background from the books: gradual emancipation was the older, slower path favored by some earlier reformers; Garrison rejects anything gradual here.
rationales.B: Garrison rules out every middle step — no equivocating, no excusing, no retreating — so his approach is abolition now, not someday.
rationales.C: Background from the books: colonization was the American Colonization Society’s plan; Garrison attacked it, and his words here demand an end to slavery itself.
rationales.D: Garrison demands action now, not patience; waiting for slavery to fade is the opposite of his pledge.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the absolutes: harsh as truth, uncompromising as justice, not one inch of retreat.
2. Ask what those absolutes rule out: gradual plans, waiting, and compromise all need the give that Garrison refuses.
3. Name what is left: an end to slavery demanded at once, in full.
Remember: when a reformer swears off every middle step, the position is immediatism, not patience.
